title: Compare the books themselves
source_text: Εἴποιμεν δ᾿ ἂν προκαλούμενοι βίβλους βίβλοις παραβάλλεσθαι ὅτι φέρε, ὦ οὗτος. τὰ Λίνου καὶ Μουσαίου καὶ Ὀρφέως ποιήματα καὶ Φερεκύδου τὴν γραφὴν καὶ συνεξέταζε τοῖς Μωϋσέως νόμοις. ἱστορίας ἱστορίαις καὶ ἠθικοὺς λόγους νόμοις καὶ προστάγμασι παρατιθείς· καὶ ὅρα ὁποῖα μᾶλλον ἐπιστρέψαι δύναται καὶ αὐτόθεν τοὺς ἀκούοντας, καὶ τίνα αὐτῶν κἂν ἐπιτρῖψαι τὸν ἀκροατήν· καὶ κατανόει ὅπως τὸ μὲν τάγμα τῶν σῶν συγγραφέων ὀλίγον μὲν ἐφρόντισε τῶν αὐτόθεν ἐντευξομένων. μόνοις δὲ ἄρα τοῖς τροπολογῆσαι καὶ ἀλληγορῆσαι δυναμένοις ἔγραψε τὴν ἰδίαν, ὡς φῇς, φιλοσοφίαν. ὁ δὲ Μω(??)σῆς ἀνάλογον γενναίῳ ῥήτορι σχῆμα μελετῶντι καὶ πανταχοῦ τὴν διπλόην τῆς λέξεως πεφυλαγμένως προφερομένῳ ἐπὶ τῶν πέντε βιβλίων πεποίηκε, μήτε τῷ πλήθει τῶν νομο θετουμένων Ἰουδαίων διδοὺς ἀφορμὰς βλάβης ἐν τῷ ἠθικῷ τόπῳ, μήτε τοῖς ὀλίγοις καὶ συνετώτερον ἐντυγχάνειν δυναμένοις οὐχὶ πλήρη θεωρίας ἐκτιθέμενος, τοῖς ἐρευνᾶν τὸ βούλημα αὐτοῦ δυναμένοις, γραφήν. καὶ τῶν μὲν σοφῶν σου ποιητῶν ἔοικε μηδὲ τὰ βιβλία ἔτι σῴζεσθαι, φυλαχθέντα ἂν, εἰ ὁ ἐντυγχάνων ᾔσθετο ὠφελείας· τοῦ δὲ Μωϋσέως τὰ γράμματα πολλοὺς καὶ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τῆς παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἀναστροφῆς κεκίνηκε πιστεῦσαι, ὅτι κατὰ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν τῶν γραμμάτων ὁ πρῶτος αὐτὰ νομοθετήσας καὶ Μωϋσεῖ παραδοὺς θεὸς ὁ κτίσας τὸν κόσμον ἦν. καὶ γὰρ ἔπρεπε τὸν ὅλου τοῦ κόσμου δημιουργὸν, νόμους τεθειμένον ὅλῳ τῷ κόσμῳ, δύναμιν παρασχεῖν τοῖς λόγοις. κρατῆσαι τῶν πανταχοῦ δυναμένην. καὶ ταῦτά φημι οὐδέπω περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐξετάζων ἀλλ᾿ ἔτι Μω(??)σέα, τὸν πολλῷ ἐλάττονα κυρίου, δεικνὺς, ὡς ὁ λόγος παραστήσει. πολλῷ διαφέροντα τῶν σοφῶν σου ποιητῶν καὶ φιλοσόφων.
pass_a_gloss: We would say, challenging (προκαλέομαι) books to be compared (παραβάλλω) with books: Come (φέρε), O you, the poems of Linus and Musaeus and Orpheus and the writing (γραφή) of Pherecydes, and examine-together (συνεξετάζω) with the laws of Moses, setting beside (παρατίθημι) histories to histories and ethical discourses (ἠθικοὶ λόγοι) to laws and commands (πρόσταγμα); and see what sort are more able to turn (ἐπιστρέφω) even straightway (αὐτόθεν) the hearers, and which of them might even wear out/ruin (ἐπιτρίβω) the listener; and consider (κατανοέω) how the order/company (τάγμα) of your writers took little thought (φροντίζω) for those who would read (ἐντυγχάνω) straightforwardly (αὐτόθεν), but only for those able to interpret figuratively and allegorise wrote their own, as you say, philosophy. But Moses, analogously to a noble orator practising (μελετάω) figure (σχῆμα) and everywhere guardedly (πεφυλαγμένως) putting forth the doubleness (διπλόη) of diction (λέξις), has done [this] in the five books, neither giving to the multitude of the legislated Jews starting-points (ἀφορμή) of harm (βλάβη) in the ethical area (ἠθικὸς τόπος), nor setting out for the few who are able to read more intelligently (συνετώτερον) a writing not full of contemplation (θεωρία), for those able to search out (ἐρευνάω) his intent (βούλημα). And of your wise poets it seems not even the books are still preserved (σῴζω), which would have been guarded if the reader had perceived (αἰσθάνομαι) benefit (ὠφέλεια); but the letters/writings (γράμματα) of Moses have moved (κινέω) many even of those foreign (ἀλλότριος) to the Jewish way of life (ἀναστροφή) to believe that, according to the profession (ἐπαγγελία) of the writings, the one who first legislated them and delivered them to Moses was God who created (κτίζω) the world. For it was fitting (πρέπει) that the craftsman (δημιουργός) of the whole world, having laid down laws for the whole world, should furnish power (δύναμις) to the words able to prevail over (κρατέω) those everywhere. And these things I say not yet examining about Jesus, but still showing Moses, the far lesser than the Lord (κύριος), as the argument will establish (παρίστημι), to be far surpassing (διαφέρω) your wise poets and philosophers.
pass_b_english: We would say, challenging him to set book beside book: “Bring out, sir, the poems of Linus, Musaeus and Orpheus and the writing of Pherecydes, and examine them together with the laws of Moses, setting histories beside histories, and moral discourses beside laws and commandments. See which are better able to turn those who hear them, even at the first hearing, and which of them might even ruin the listener. Observe how the company of your writers cared little for those who would read them in the plain sense, and wrote their own philosophy, as you say, only for those able to interpret it figuratively and allegorically. Moses, on the other hand, in his five books has acted like a noble orator who studies the figures of speech and everywhere puts forward the double sense of his wording with care: he neither gave the mass of the Jews under his law occasions of harm in matters of conduct, nor set before the few who are able to read with greater understanding, those who can search out his intent, a writing lacking in contemplation.

“And it seems that the books of your wise poets are not even preserved any longer, though they would have been kept if the reader had perceived any benefit. But the writings of Moses have moved many, even of those foreign to the Jewish way of life, to believe that, as the writings themselves declare, the One who first gave them as law and delivered them to Moses was God, who created the world. For it was fitting that the Maker of the whole world, who had laid down laws for the whole world, should give his words a power able to prevail over people everywhere. And I say this not yet examining the case of Jesus, but still showing that Moses, who is far less than the Lord, far surpasses, as the argument will establish, your wise poets and philosophers.”

choices.choice: Staged Greek shows '(??)' inside Μωϋσῆς and its cases (Μω(??)υσῆς, Μω(??)σέως): an encoding artefact for the diaeresis, no textual effect. Staged text splits νομο θετουμένων (read νομοθετουμένων). 'μήτε ... οὐχὶ πλήρη θεωρίας ἐκτιθέμενος ... γραφήν' is a double negative: Moses did not fail to give the few a writing full of contemplation; rendered 'nor set before the few ... a writing lacking in contemplation', keeping the negative form. 'αὐτόθεν' is used twice: first 'even at the first hearing' (immediately, by itself), then 'in the plain sense' (readers taking the text at face value). 'σχῆμα μελετῶντι' = practising rhetorical figure; 'διπλόη τῆς λέξεως' = double sense of the wording. 'ἐπαγγελία τῶν γραμμάτων' = what the writings profess, rendered 'as the writings themselves declare'. 'τὸν πολλῷ ἐλάττονα κυρίου' (Moses far less than the Lord) may echo Hebrews 3:3 (Jesus counted worthy of more glory than Moses), but that is only a possible allusion and is not cited inline. The placement of 'as the argument will establish' follows the Greek, attaching it to Moses' superiority over the poets.
φέρε ... καὶ συνεξέταζε: 'Come, sir, bring' (doubled) -> 'Bring out, sir, ... and examine' (φέρε is the verb paired by καί)
τὴν διπλόην τῆς λέξεως πεφυλαγμένως προφερομένῳ: 'sets forth his words with careful attention to their double meaning' -> 'puts forward the double sense of his wording with care'
appositive τοῖς ἐρευνᾶν τὸ βούλημα αὐτοῦ δυναμένοις moved beside 'the few' instead of trailing after 'writing' (removes Greek word order)
εἰ ὁ ἐντυγχάνων: 'those who read them' -> 'the reader' (singular as in the Greek)
address to Celsus runs through both paragraphs (σου in paragraph 2): quotation marks fixed so it opens each paragraph and closes only at the end
possible echo of Hebrews 3:3 in 'far less than the Lord' left uncited: not a clear allusion
